# Job 29 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

Job 29 is the first part of Job's final summary defense (chs. 29–31). After a pause waiting for his friends to reply—and none does—Job resumes his discourse with a wistful retrospect of his former blessedness. He describes three areas: (1) his intimate relationship with God (vv. 2–6), (2) the honour he enjoyed in the community because of his righteous deeds (vv. 7–17), and (3) his former confidence and authority (vv. 18–25). The chapter forms a deliberate contrast with chapter 30, where he laments his present misery.

---

## Verse-by-Verse Notes

**v. 1 — "And Job continued his discourse:"**
Job paused, waiting for any reply from his three friends. Hearing none, he resumed speaking. This second address is not so much an answer to the friends as a statement of his whole case as he saw it. (Enduring Word, citing Morgan) The chapter heading in the Hebrew is literally "Job continued his parable" (KJV), meaning a weighty, proverbial discourse. (Gill)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-29/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/29.htm

**v. 2 — "How I long for the months gone by, for the days when God watched over me,"**
Job's deepest sorrow was not material but spiritual: he felt that God no longer watched over him. The word translated "watched over" (or in KJV, "preserved") indicates God's protective care from calamity. Job's keenest lament is the loss of felt divine preservation. Gill notes this may be a wish for the return of spiritual prosperity—the presence and favour of God—not merely outward wealth. (Enduring Word; JFB; Gill)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-29/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/29.htm

**v. 3 — "when His lamp shone above my head, and by His light I walked through the darkness,"**
The "lamp" or "candle" signifies God's favour shining upon Job. By God's light, Job passed safely through dangers—Noyes suggests an allusion to torches carried before caravans in night travels through deserts. Spurgeon saw here the loss of divine consolation: Job once had God's lamp upon his head, and now it seemed gone. He also lost divine illumination—by God's light, perplexity had ceased to be perplexity. (JFB; Enduring Word citing Spurgeon)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-29/

**v. 4 — "when I was in my prime, when the friendship of God rested on my tent,"**
The Hebrew literally reads "in the days of my autumn"—the season of ripe fruits, picturing mature prosperity. The "friendship" or "secret" (KJV) of God means intimate, confidential fellowship, as in Proverbs 3:32; Psalm 25:14; John 15:15. The Pulpit Commentary says: "The word 'secret' means intimacy, confidential intercourse. God was near to him." JFB notes the Hebrew word for "secret" often means a divan or council for deliberation—God's intimate counsel rested on Job's home. Ellicott translates it "the counsel of God." This was the loss of divine communion that Spurgeon highlighted. (Ellicott; JFB; Pulpit Homiletics; Enduring Word)
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/29.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/29.htm

**v. 5 — "when the Almighty was still with me and my children were around me,"**
Job recalls God's special gracious presence—not mere providential presence, but the felt nearness of the Almighty. Alongside this, his children (and possibly servants, as the Hebrew word can mean both—Gill notes this) surrounded him. Now both God's felt presence and his children were gone. (Gill)
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/29.htm

**v. 6 — "when my steps were bathed in cream and the rock poured out for me streams of oil!"**
Hyperbolic imagery from pastoral life depicting extraordinary abundance. "Cream" (literally "thick milk")—wherever Job walked, the richest provision flowed to him. Oil from the rock: olives grown on rocky terrain produce the best oil. It does not mean he literally washed his feet in butter; rather, abundance was so great that such a thing was imaginable. Oil was used for food, light, anointing, and medicine in the ancient Near East. Deuteronomy 32:13 uses similar imagery for God's provision to Israel. (JFB; Gill; Ellicott)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/29.htm

**v. 7 — "When I went out to the city gate and took my seat in the public square,"**
The city gate was the place of judgment and public administration in the ancient Near East (Deut 21:19; 22:15; Josh 20:4). The "public square" (or "open square" / "street") was the broad open place near the gate where court was held. Job, as a chief magistrate or elder, would process from his house through the city to take his judicial seat. (JFB; Gill; Ellicott; Dunagan)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/29.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/job-29.html

**v. 8 — "the young men saw me and withdrew, and the old men rose to their feet."**
Young men stepped back or hid themselves out of reverential awe (perhaps also fearing his scrutiny of their conduct). The aged—already seated—rose and remained standing until Job took his seat. This reflects ancient Near Eastern customs of honouring a superior. (JFB; Gill; Enduring Word)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/29.htm

**v. 9 — "The princes refrained from speaking and covered their mouths with their hands."**
Even "princes" (or chiefs, leaders) stopped mid-sentence when Job arrived, laying a hand over the mouth as a gesture of silence and deference. (JFB; Job 21:5 uses the same gesture.)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html

**v. 10 — "The voices of the nobles were hushed, and their tongues stuck to the roofs of their mouths."**
"Nobles" may refer to military commanders or men of high birth—even these bold men were awed into total silence. Their "voice was hid" (margin); their tongues cleaved to the roof of the mouth—a vivid image of speechlessness, also found in Ezekiel 3:26. Gill comments that this silence was either from fear of being exposed by Job's superior wisdom, or from eagerness to hear his opinion first. (JFB; Gill)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/29.htm

**v. 11 — "For those who heard me called me blessed, and those who saw me commended me,"**
Ellicott notes this is a direct negative to Eliphaz's charges in Job 22:6ff—Job felt those accusations deeply and now refutes them, though indirectly. Whoever heard about Job praised him ("blessed" him); whoever saw him face-to-face gave witness to his honourable character. The ear/eye contrast is deliberate: both by reputation and by direct observation, Job was esteemed. (Ellicott; JFB; Enduring Word)
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/29.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html

**v. 12 — "because I rescued the poor who cried out and the fatherless who had no helper."**
The reason for Job's public esteem: his active compassion. He delivered the poor from their oppressors. The fatherless (orphan) had "none to help"—a phrase noting the power imbalance—and Job stepped in as their defender. This answers Eliphaz's false accusations in Job 22:6–9. (JFB; Gill; Enduring Word)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/29.htm

**v. 13 — "The dying man blessed me, and I made the widow's heart sing for joy."**
"The dying man" (or "him who was ready to perish," KJV) — those on the brink of death blessed Job for his rescue. Widows, often the most vulnerable, had their hearts filled with singing because of his intervention. JFB notes: "So far was I from sending widows away empty (Job 22:9)." (JFB; Enduring Word)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html

**v. 14 — "I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; justice was my robe and my turban."**
Righteousness and justice were so characteristic of Job that they seemed like garments he wore. The "robe" (outer flowing mantle) and "turban" (head-dress or tiara) were the distinctive dress of an Oriental grandee or high priest. Ellicott gives a striking insight: the Hebrew literally reads "it clothed itself with me"—first righteousness is the garment, then Job becomes the garment for righteousness. He sees a foreshadowing of the Gospel truth of the interchange between Christ and the believer: Christ bears our sins, we are clothed with His righteousness. (JFB; Ellicott; Dunagan)
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/29.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/job-29.html

**v. 15 — "I served as eyes to the blind and as feet to the lame."**
Job guided those who could not see and supported those who could not walk. JFB notes this can be taken both literally (Deut 27:18; 2 Sam 9:13) and figuratively—spiritual guidance to the less enlightened (cf. Job 4:3; Heb 12:13). (JFB; Gill; Enduring Word)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html

**v. 16 — "I was a father to the needy, and I took up the case of the stranger."**
A direct rebuttal of Eliphaz's accusation that Job "broke the arms of the fatherless" (Job 22:9). Job was instead a father to the needy. "The stranger"—literally "him whom I knew not"—Job took up the legal cause of complete strangers, searching out the facts to ensure justice. This shows conscientious judicial investigation, not mere superficial charity. (JFB; Gill; Dunagan; Enduring Word)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/29.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/job-29.html

**v. 17 — "I shattered the fangs of the unjust and snatched the prey from his teeth."**
Vivid imagery of a wild beast: Job broke the power (jaws/fangs) of the wicked oppressor so he could do no more harm, and tore the victim from his teeth. Job was compassionate to the oppressed and terrible to the oppressor. Strauss comments: "Job rescued the poor from their ruthless oppressors, but he also destroyed the power of the aggressor." (JFB; Dunagan citing Strauss; Gill)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/job-29.html

**v. 18 — "So I thought: 'I will die in my nest and multiply my days as the sand.'"**
In his former confidence, Job expected to die peacefully, surrounded by family ("in my nest"—a secure dwelling), after a long life. The phrase "multiply my days as the sand" uses sand as a figure for innumerable abundance (Gen 22:17). However, JFB notes that the Septuagint, Vulgate, and some rabbinic interpreters translate "sand" (Hebrew *hol*) as the phoenix bird—a legendary creature that lived 500 years, died in a nest of myrrh, and rose again. The parallel "nest" supports the bird reference, though most modern translations retain "sand." Constable notes this phoenix interpretation was argued in a Catholic Biblical Quarterly article (Heras, 1949). Job did eventually realize his hope (Job 42:16–17, where he lived 140 more years and died "old and full of days"). (JFB; Enduring Word citing Smick; Constable)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-29/

**v. 19 — "My roots will spread out to the waters, and the dew will rest nightly on my branches."**
Metaphor of a healthy, well-watered tree (cf. Psalm 1:3; Jer 17:8): roots open to abundant water, dew refreshing the branches each night. The image conveys continual nourishment, vigour, and divine blessing. JFB notes this is opposed to the fate of the wicked in Job 18:16, whose roots dry up. (JFB; Enduring Word citing Clarke)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-29/

**v. 20 — "My glory is ever new within me, and my bow is renewed in my hand."**
"Glory" (or renown/honour) remained continually fresh. The "bow" is a metaphor from warfare for strength and vigour (cf. Gen 49:24; Jer 49:35; 1 Sam 2:4)—Job's manly strength was constantly renewed, never failing. (JFB; Ellicott; Enduring Word)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/29.htm

**v. 21 — "Men listened to me with expectation, waiting silently for my counsel."**
Job returns to describing the deference he commanded. Men waited in attentive silence, eager for his words. This picks up the theme from vv. 7–10. (JFB; Enduring Word)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html

**v. 22 — "After my words, they spoke no more; my speech settled on them like dew."**
Once Job had spoken, no one contradicted or added to his words. His speech was gentle yet penetrating, settling on the hearers like dew—refreshing, life-giving, gently persuasive (cf. Deut 32:2; Song 4:11). This contrasts sharply with the friends' harsh words. (JFB; Enduring Word)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html

**v. 23 — "They waited for me as for rain and drank in my words like spring showers."**
The image intensifies: people thirsted for Job's counsel as dry ground thirsts for rain. They "opened their mouth wide" (as the Hebrew has it), panting for his words. The "spring rain" (or "latter rain," March rains) brought the harvest to maturity and was eagerly awaited in an agricultural society (Deut 11:14; James 5:7). (JFB; Enduring Word)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html

**v. 24 — "If I smiled at them, they did not believe it; the light of my countenance was precious."**
Two main interpretations exist. (1) When Job relaxed his gravity and smiled, people could hardly believe such condescension—they were so in awe of him. Yet they did not lose their reverence ("cast down his countenance"). (2) Umbreit's translation: "I smiled kindly on those who trusted not"—Job cheered the despondent, and their despondency could not cast down his serene confidence in God. The "light of my countenance" refers to his favour and encouragement; Poole says people found his approval so precious they could scarcely believe it when he showed it. (JFB; Enduring Word citing Poole)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-29/

**v. 25 — "I chose their course and presided as chief. So I dwelt as a king among his troops, as a comforter of the mourners."**
Job "chose their way"—he directed and decided the course for the community. He "sat as chief" (or "dwelt as chief"), exercising supreme authority like a king among his army. Yet remarkably, his final self-description is not as ruler but as "one who comforts mourners." Ellicott observes: it is still Jewish custom for mourners to sit on the ground while the comforter sits above them. JFB and Ellicott both see here an unconscious foreshadowing of Christ—who is both King and the Comforter of those who mourn (Isa 61:2–3; Isa 50:4; Heb 2:18). Job's afflictions were fitting him for this very office. (JFB; Ellicott; Enduring Word)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/29.htm

---

## Tradition-Specific Notes

### Reformed / Presbyterian

Reformed commentators emphasise that Job's lament reveals the primacy of spiritual loss over material loss. Spurgeon, cited extensively in Enduring Word (which draws on broadly Reformed sources), outlined four losses Job felt: divine preservation, divine consolation, divine illumination, and divine communion. The loss of felt nearness to God is the darkest darkness. Ligonier's devotionals on Job highlight the hidden wisdom of God in suffering and point toward Job's ultimate restoration and vindication (Job 42). (Though no Ligonier page specifically on Job 29 was retrieved, their general approach to Job is evident in devotionals on Job's repentance and restoration.)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-29/
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jobs-repentance-and-restoration

### Baptist

John Gill (1746–63), a Reformed Baptist, offers extensive notes. He interprets v. 2 as a wish possibly for the return of spiritual prosperity—frames of soul, exercise of grace, and communion with God—rather than merely outward wealth. He notes that "children" (v. 5) may include servants, and gives detailed spiritual applications, e.g., that Christ the Rock pours out rivers of oil (the Holy Spirit). Gill also notes that some read "secret of God" in v. 4 as "assembly of God"—the gathering of saints in Job's tent for worship. Charles Spurgeon's sermon insights (quoted in Enduring Word) reflect the Baptist emphasis on personal communion with God and the anguish of losing it.
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/29.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-29/

### Pentecostal / Charismatic

David Guzik's Enduring Word commentary (broadly charismatic/evangelical) emphasises the felt loss of God's presence as Job's keenest sorrow and notes that Job used his wealth for others, not selfish indulgence. Guzik highlights that Job had shown "enormous restraint" in not pointing to good works until now—taking his stand on faith alone. The application calls readers to recognise that true leadership flows from genuine care for others.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-29/

### Anglican

Charles Ellicott's Commentary for English Readers (1905) provides careful philological notes. On v. 14, Ellicott draws a distinctively Gospel-oriented conclusion: "This is the Gospel truth of the interchange of sin and righteousness between Christ and the believer. He bears our sins; we are clothed with the robe of His righteousness." On v. 25, Ellicott calls Job "the type and representative of suffering humanity, of man waiting for redemption, but as yet unredeemed," pointing to Christ. On v. 1, he references Ecclesiastes 7:10 as a caution against romanticising the past.
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/29.htm

### Brethren / Plymouth Brethren

Grant's Commentary (on StudyLight) takes a distinctive line: while Job spoke truthfully, "there is far too much of 'self' in what he says," contrasting chapter 29 unfavourably with chapter 28 where Job gave God His proper place. Grant suggests Job exposed the pride of his self-importance, "revealing why it was necessary for God to bring him down," and cites Philippians 3:7, 13–14 as the Christian antidote—forgetting what lies behind. He also notes John 5:41: "I do not receive honour from men."
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-29.html

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship: The "Phoenix" in v. 18

Multiple commentators note an alternative translation for "as the sand" (Hebrew *hol*). The Septuagint (Greek OT) and Vulgate (Latin) read "as the palm" or understand it as the phoenix bird. The phoenix was a mythical bird said to live 500 years, die in a nest of myrrh, and be reborn. Dr. Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary, broadly evangelical/dispensational) notes that Henry Heras argued for this reading in the *Catholic Biblical Quarterly* (1949). The parallel "nest" in the same verse makes the bird imagery plausible, though most modern translations retain "sand." Smick (cited in Enduring Word) says, "The question seems to hinge on whether the word *hol* (usually 'sand') can mean 'phoenix' at all." JFB gives the fullest account of the phoenix legend and suggests Job probably refers to it.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-29.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-29/

### Catholic Reading

No specifically Catholic page on Job 29 was retrieved from newadvent.org or catholic.com. However, the JFB commentary's reference to the Vulgate's rendering of v. 18 (the phoenix) and the *Catholic Biblical Quarterly* article indicate Catholic scholarly engagement with the passage. The Vulgate's interpretive tradition tends to read v. 18 through the lens of the phoenix as a symbol of resurrection.

### Orthodox Reading

No Orthodox-specific page on Job 29 from oca.org was retrieved in the searches.

### Prosperity / Word of Faith Teaching

No pages from the allowed sites addressed a prosperity-gospel reading of Job 29. However, it is worth noting that vv. 2–6, with their language of abundant cream, oil, and God's blessing, could be (and sometimes are) cited in prosperity teaching as a model of the blessed life God intends. The traditional commentaries consistently read these verses as describing Job's *former* state—a memory, not a permanent promise—and note that Job's blessing flowed from his relationship with God and his righteous care for others, not from a mechanistic "formula" of faith.

---

## Summary of Key Themes

- **Spiritual loss above material loss**: Job's deepest lament is for the felt presence and favour of God, not for his lost wealth (vv. 2–5). Spurgeon: "No darkness is so dark as that which falls on eyes accustomed to the light."

- **Righteousness expressed in social justice**: Job's honour was not from status but from active compassion—defending the poor, the orphan, the widow, the blind, the lame, and the stranger (vv. 12–17). This refutes his friends' accusations.

- **Fragility of earthly confidence**: Job's assumption that he would "die in his nest" (v. 18) proved naive. His security was overturned, teaching that earthly prosperity is never guaranteed.

- **Christological foreshadowing**: Several commentators see Job as a type of Christ—the righteous sufferer who was eyes to the blind, feet to the lame, a father to the needy, and ultimately the comforter of mourners (v. 25).

- **The danger of self-exaltation**: Grant's commentary warns that even truthfully recounting one's virtues can reflect pride, and that the Christian is called to forget what lies behind (Phil 3:13–14).
